limitations: All 71 PDF pages were examined in extracted text, including five chapters, introduction and conclusion. The cover has no extractable text and was examined visually. Seventeen selected pages received visual inspection; four critical pages were also inspected at larger size. Remaining illustrations did not receive a separate visual engineering audit.

The cover is unnumbered: its ledger book_page is null. Visible printed pages 2-71 equal one-based PDF pages 2-71. Chapter 0 spans PDF 1-12 and printed 2-12. All item citations use actual printed pages; no record invents a printed cover number.

Records count coherent reusable claims, procedures, recipes or inventory/table entries. Each of the seven fermentation recipes, five pickle recipes, four drying-temperature rows and ten root-cellar rows is separately represented. Repeated principles in different sections remain traceable; these are not 142 unique household tasks or shopping items.

Original text is paraphrased with exact inclusive page spans. Recipe quantities are retained as source claims, not executable instructions. The omission of required specifications is documented rather than filled with invented quantities or times.

Verified guidance is a narrow supported statement and does not certify the surrounding recipe or chapter. None of the seven fermentation or five pickle recipes is verified. Source-derived reference is not a safety endorsement. All records remain execution-ineligible and proposed milestone mappings do not establish household preparedness capacity.

Evidence was checked on October 31, 2026. F13 and F22 use accessible primary-source indexed article text because direct USDA article opens timed out; those are explicitly marked primary_excerpt_reviewed and do not support any verified record. Other cited sources were content-reviewed. Immutable external snapshots were not archived.

Virginia Cooperative Extension food-storage and fermentation guidance was used for local relevance. No property-specific building, excavation, permit, commercial food-sale or Virginia regulatory determination was performed. EPA and USGS water-specific checks were not relevant to these food-preservation instructions; FDA and CDC cover relevant federal health issues.

Many historical claims, yield/price comparisons, nutritional superiority, shelf-life estimates and product-performance assertions remain unverified. No batch was cooked, cultured, canned, measured for pH/water activity, laboratory-tested or field-tested. Structural and rendering gaps are reviewer analyses, not externally validated replacement designs or recipes.

Schema v1.2.0 preserves earlier datasets and additionally supports null unnumbered ledger pages and an explicit primary-source excerpt access status. Schemas and finalized outputs for Books 1 and 2 remain unchanged.

No HomePrep app, LPI code, database import, deployment, purchasing or external messaging was performed. The other agent’s LPI work is a separate phase; this work updates examination artifacts and the library tracker only.

record.title: Canning needs a tested process, not merely a seal
record.guidance: Reject 158 F for 20 minutes as a universal sterilization rule. Low-acid home-canned food needs an appropriate tested pressure-canning process. Follow the exact food, formulation, preparation, pack, jar, headspace, time, pressure and altitude requirements. A pop, concave lid or intact seal does not prove adequate processing. No arbitrary recipe is made safe by substituting an invented pressure-canning time.

record.title: Jars, failed seals and pressure-canner operation
record.guidance: Use the selected tested process and equipment/lid directions. Where empty-jar presterilization is required, NCHFP specifies boiling water and elevation adjustment; 158 F is inadequate as the stated method. Pressure canners need ten minutes of free steam venting, correct altitude-adjusted operation, full processing time and natural cooling. If pressure drops, restart the full time. Seal failure requires prompt appropriate handling; eligible reprocessing uses a new lid and full correct process within 24 hours. This is not a rescue rule for initially unsafe food.

record.title: Drying is not a substitute for validated heating and endpoints
record.guidance: Use food-specific tested preparation, heating, drying and storage directions. Uncontrolled raw-meat sun drying and a 155 F air setting do not establish a safe internal heat treatment. Refrigerate jerky marination; do not infer a microbial kill from dryness, firmness or color. Outdoor sun drying is limited to suitable foods and favorable weather, rather than all meat and vegetables. Jerky shelf life cannot be inferred from the author’s months-long anecdote.

record.title: Salt-fish procedure has unresolved controls
record.guidance: The source omits a measured food-grade salt formulation, fish-specific handling, safe holding temperature, drying endpoint and validated keeping conditions. Rock or ice-cream-maker salt is not established as suitable for food by that description. The reviewer has not supplied a replacement salt-fish recipe; obtain a tested fish-specific method before use.

record.title: Reject oven dry canning
record.guidance: Do not use the book’s lidded-jar, twelve-hour oven process or reheat failed seals as a preservation method. NCHFP does not recommend oven or dry canning. Independently, the unit conversion is wrong: (200-32) times 5/9 is about 93.3 C, not 70 C. The author’s own lack-of-proof warning does not validate the procedure.

record.title: Pickles and ferments require food-specific controls
record.guidance: Retain tested food-to-liquid proportions and the recipe’s specified vinegar acidity, salt, temperature, fermentation completion, processing and storage requirements. Do not use tanginess or submersion alone as a safety test. The seven book ferments lack adequate process specifications; a small cabbage count is not a weight-based salt formulation. For comparison, F08 uses three tablespoons of salt per five pounds of shredded cabbage and describes about three to four weeks at 70-75 F, with its full handling and storage directions still required. This is a separate tested method, not a validated edit of the book recipe. The five quick-pickle recipes omit essential controls. Pickled eggs must be refrigerated; no recommended home-canning method makes these eggs pantry-stable.

record.title: Smoking and curing do not automatically make shelf-stable meat
record.guidance: Use a validated food-specific cure and process, the correct measured curing product and dose, refrigerated handling, an internal food thermometer and appropriate post-process storage. A premix is not self-dosing. Smoker-air temperature, dark color, a supposed impermeable pellicle or re-smoking a cut surface cannot demonstrate safety. USDA’s reviewed smoking-storage excerpt directs refrigeration within two hours, use within four days or freezing. No complete alternative shelf-stable curing recipe is supplied here.

record.title: Oxygen-reduced packaging is only for suitable dry foods
record.guidance: Do not equate absence of oxygen with absence of microbial hazards. USU warns about botulism with moist food in reduced-oxygen packages and describes about 10% or less moisture for this dry-storage context. That limit alone does not certify every product or a universal shelf life. Use known suitable food-contact containers, a food-appropriate packaging specification, clean equipment and manufacturer-sized absorbers. White color, a rat anecdote, a vacuum-cleaner hose or a nominal absorber size is not validation.

record.title: Measure cold storage and match the crop
record.guidance: A root cellar or evaporative cooler is not a refrigerator unless measured conditions support the food’s requirements. VCE calls for refrigerated food below 40 F; a 55 F claim is inadequate for general perishables. Match produce variety, humidity, temperature, curing and ventilation rather than treating the chart’s durations as guarantees. F15 describes very moist apple and pear storage rather than the book’s undefined medium humidity. UMN gives around 50-55 F for winter squash and pumpkins. The older WSU bulletin itself has different generalized and crop-specific squash ranges; these are not interchangeable universal prescriptions. Freezer burn concerns quality; it does not by itself make food unsafe.

record.title: Shelf life and date labels are conditional
record.guidance: Most commercial date labels concern quality, with infant formula an exception. Proper storage and the actual product matter. No seal or date establishes perpetual safety. For home-canned food, authoritative labeling, storage and best-quality guidance should be used instead of the book’s indefinite-life reassurance.

record.title: Avoid blanket anti-preservative and untested-GMO claims
record.guidance: FDA describes both antimicrobial and antioxidant preservative functions, rather than a merely cosmetic role. FDA, EPA and USDA have regulatory roles for genetically engineered foods, including FDA’s voluntary product-by-product consultation and submitted safety assessment data. These sources do not support the book’s blanket size-based harm argument or absence-of-assessment claim.

record.title: Underground storage sketches are not construction plans
record.guidance: Excavation, earth loads, drainage, access, structural support, materials and entrapment hazards remain unresolved. A block lining or buried refrigerator sketch is not evidence of a safe structure. Obtain a qualified site-specific design before construction; this examination does not determine permits or code compliance.

record.title: Home-rendered lard shelf stability is not established
record.guidance: The source supplies no validated moisture endpoint, process specification or storage study. Pale color does not resolve that gap. No universal room-temperature shelf life is assigned. Obtain a tested rendering and storage method, or qualified food-preservation advice; this examination does not assert that all properly rendered lard requires refrigeration.
